bibliographic.abstract: Laser metal additive manufacturing technology is capable of producing components with complex geometries and compositions that cannot be realized by conventional manufacturing methods. However, a large number of pores generated during the additive manufacturing process greatly affect the mechanical properties of the additively manufactured parts, and the mechanism of such pore generation has not been revealed by direct observation clearly. Here, we report the mechanism of pore generation in the laser direct energy deposition process as revealed by in-situ high-speed high-resolution synchrotron X-ray imaging. We found that dissolution and re-precipitation of external gases and precipitation of metal vapors are the two main mechanisms of pore formation. We further explored the effects of different process parameters on the generation of pores and optimized the process to suppress pore generation. This work provides important insights into the formation of porosity defects during laser metal additive manufacturing, and can provide guidance for related process optimization.

samples.sample_description: Bare plate with 0.6 mm thickness used in laser directed energy deposition.
Formed sample produced by laser directed energy deposition of Al2024 alloy.

datasets.dataset_description: A stationary high-energy synchrotron X-ray beam at beamline 3W1 penetrated through the specimen from horizontal direction during laser scanning; transmitted X-rays were converted by a LuAG:Ce scintillator and recorded by a high-speed camera with a frame rate of 2000 Hz and spatial resolution of 4 µm per pixel.
X-ray computed tomography at Beamline 18U1 using 25 keV monochromatic x-rays; the voxel size after CT reconstruction is 1.6 µm.
Scanning electron microscope and energy dispersive spectroscopy were used to characterize slices against the formed specimens and the internal elemental composition of bubbles.
datasets.measurement_technique: scanning electron microscope and energy dispersive spectroscopy
